item.title: An upper bound for the three-dimensional moving sofa problem in a snaky corridor
item.description: arXiv:2610.14050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $K_M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the "snaky" corridor with unit-square cross-section: an infinite entry arm parallel to the $x$-axis, a middle arm parallel to the $y$-axis whose clear straight section has length $M$, and an infinite exit arm parallel to the $z$-axis, with the two turns lying in the $x$-$y$ and $y$-$z$ planes. Let $V^*(K_M)$ be the supremum of the volumes of connected bodies that can be moved continuously (by rigid motions) from the entry arm to the exit arm while remaining inside $K_M$. We prove $V^*(K_M) \le 7.8691$ for every $M \ge 3.53$ (Theorem A); by a sharper analysis of the same mechanism, $V^*(K_M) \le 4.2862$ for every $M \ge 2.61$ (Theorem B); and, by replacing the final analytic caps with a certified branch-and-bound computation over the compact family of entry tubes compatible with the forced events, $V^*(K_M) \le 3.4083$ for every $M > 2.2$ (Theorem C; computer-assisted, in double precision with conservative slack). In particular all three bounds apply to the corridor with $M = 4$ used in Problem 6.64 of Georgiev, G\'omez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner (arXiv:2511.02864), and uniformly to every "turns far apart" reading of that problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first upper bound for the snaky-corridor 3D moving sofa problem; previously not even finiteness of $V^*$ had been recorded. This note proves upper bounds only; combined with the certified lower bound 1.8558404 from the author's separate certification work via the problem's own evaluation pipeline, the state of the problem becomes $1.8558404 \le V^*(K_4) \le 3.4083$. Theorems A and B are elementary and self-contained: a first-crossing (elbow) event forces a definite tilt of the body's own entry tube, and Fubini-type chord estimates for tilted tubes cap the volume. Theorem C certifies, by the same forced-event skeleton, the largest corridor volume that any admissible entry tube can carry.
item.dc:creator: Yuzhe Tang

item.title: New certified lower bounds for the moving sofa problem in a three-dimensional snaky corridor
item.description: arXiv:2610.14051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consider the "snaky" corridor $K_4 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ from Problem 6.64 of arXiv:2511.02864: a tube of unit-square cross-section whose two right-angle turns lie in perpendicular planes, with a straight middle section of clear length $4$. We exhibit explicit rigid motions of connected bodies through $K_4$ and certify their volumes with the problem's own evaluation pipeline, unmodified, at the tight motion tolerances of its final scoring stage (translation $0.005$, rotation $0.05$ degrees). The certificates give $V^*(K_4) \ge 1.8355162$ at grid fineness $0.002$ and $V^*(K_4) \ge 1.8558404$ at grid fineness $0.001$, against the previously reported $1.81$; rerunning the pipeline's published best path under the identical configuration yields $1.8179428$, so every comparison is path against path under one fixed certifier. Three stages produce the record motion: a simple "staggered twist" backbone in which the whole 90-degree twist about the tube axis happens inside the second turn; evolutionary (CMA-ES) refinement, including a mixed-fidelity scheme that re-scores each generation's leading candidates on a grid twice as fine and lets those ranks steer recombination; and a gradient polish carried out directly at the finer carve resolution, guarded by periodic rebuilding of the frozen interpolation structure and by a penalty on control-pose spacing. These guards close three documented failure modes in which an optimizer inflates its own objective: frozen-structure inflation, spacing stretch, and exploitation of a coarse grid by optimizing and selecting on it. A staircase-based predictor with two grid bases, anchored by matching grid sensitivity, forecast the certificates to about $0.001$ before the runs. With the companion note's upper bound $V^*(K_4) \le 3.4083$, the problem now sits in the bracket $1.8558404 \le V^*(K_4) \le 3.4083$. All paths, notebooks and certified results are public.
item.dc:creator: Yuzhe Tang

item.title: Shaving Two Logs for Discrete and Continuous Fr\'echet Distance
item.description: arXiv:2610.16360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the classical computational geometry problem of computing the exact (discrete or continuous) Fr\'echet distance between two given polygonal curves with $n$ vertices in a constant dimension $d$. 1. We present an $O((n^2/\log^2n)\log^2\log n)$-time deterministic algorithm for the discrete Fr\'echet distance problem, improving the previous $O((n^2/\log n)\log\log n)$ result by Agarwal, Ben Avraham, Kaplan, and Sharir [SODA'13]. 2. We present an $O((n^2/\log^2n)\log^2\log n)$-time deterministic algorithm for the decision version of the continuous Fr\'echet distance problem, improving the previous $O((n^2/\log n)\log^2\log n)$ result by Buchin, Buchin, Meulemans, and Mulzer [SODA'14] and the recent $O(n^2/\log^{1+\mu}n)$ randomized result by Cheng and Huang [SODA'25] for a small unspecified constant $\mu>0$ (which converges to 0 as $d$ increases). 3. Finally, we present an $O((n^2/\log^2 n)\log^{O(1)}\log n)$-time Las Vegas randomized algorithm for the continuous Fr\'echet distance problem, improving the previous $O(n^2\log^2\log n)$ randomized result by Buchin, Buchin, Meulemans, and Mulzer [SODA'14] and the recent $O(n^2/\log^{\mu}n)$-time randomized result claimed by Cheng and Huang [SODA'25]. Since these problems have near-quadratic OV-based conditional lower bounds and shaving of two log factors is the best that is known for similar, simpler problems such as longest common subsequence and edit distance, our results reach the natural limit of the current state of the art (up to $\log\log$ factors).
item.dc:creator: Timothy M Chan, Isaac M Hair

item.title: Hypergeometric Bridges for Multidimensional Grid Visibility
item.description: arXiv:2610.16795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Established interpolation-based methods efficiently compute visibility from one source to every grid cell using values computed closer to the source. Interpolation yields fractional values even on binary grids of free or fully blocking cells. Two-dimensional path-counting theory interprets these values as fractions of unobstructed grid paths, but three-dimensional methods use different predecessor structures. Interpreting these values consistently across dimensions and on nonbinary grids remains unresolved. We provide a unified mathematical account that gives every visibility value a precise meaning in any dimension. We establish when grid refinement yields eventual agreement with continuous visibility, implement parallel solvers, and compare four three-dimensional methods in accuracy and throughput. We define cell transmission: zero blocks visibility, one preserves it, and intermediate values attenuate it proportionally. We prove each computed value equals the uniform finite-path average of transmission products over finitely many source-to-cell grid paths. It is the fraction of clear paths on binary grids and the mean path transmission on nonbinary grids. For a source--target query, the fractions of paths passing through cells at each step form a hypergeometric distribution in 2D, which we call the hypergeometric bridge. On the last step into the target, these probabilities equal the interpolation weights. Higher-dimensional interpolation weights arise from products of hypergeometric bridges. For any fixed dimension, the full-field algorithm remains linear in grid size. Exact path enumeration reproduces every checked visibility value. NumPy, OpenMP, and CUDA agree numerically, and our OpenMP solver achieves the highest throughput in the four-method CPU comparison at every tested resolution.
item.dc:creator: Ibrahim Ibrahim, Wilm Decr\'e

item.title: The Rhythm of the Tiles: Narrow and Low Temperature Computation and Simulation in Synchronous Tile Self-Assembly
item.description: arXiv:2610.17112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we prove that the synchronicity provided by the syncTAM can be leveraged to perform two additional feats impossible in the asynchronous aTAM. The aTAM has long been known to be equivalent to finite automata in the one-dimensional case. For our first set of results, we prove that this still holds when a finite, fixed amount of space is available in the second dimension. Yet, surprisingly, in the synchronous setting, a small, fixed, width is enough to simulate a Turing Machine. This holds even in the non-cooperative setting. For our second set of main results we prove that there exists a single set of syncTAM tiles that can be used to simulate any syncTAM system simply by using those tiles to create a scaled version of the seed structure of the original system and then letting the tiles from that set self-assemble from the scaled seed structure. While it has been shown (FOCS 2012) that such a tile set also exists in the aTAM for simulating all aTAM systems, that "intrinsically universal" (IU) tile set requires cooperativity (and is impossible without cooperativity as shown in SODA 2014). We prove there exists an IU tile set in the syncTAM that works without cooperativity. Furthermore, there exists a tile set that is IU for the class of directed systems (i.e. systems which each have a single terminal assembly) while remaining directed during simulation. This was shown to be impossible in the aTAM (FOCS 2016).
item.dc:creator: Florent Becker, Phillip Drake, Benjamin Durbin, Nicolas Ollinger, Brent Orlina, Matthew J. Patitz

item.title: Optimal Planar $k$ Nearest Neighbors Queries for Additively Weighted Euclidean Distances and Convex Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.17430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a set $P$ of $n$ point sites in the plane, the $k$ nearest neighbors problem is to build a data structure that, for a query point $v$ and a query integer $k$, reports the $k$ nearest point sites of $v$ in $P$ efficiently. For the Euclidean metric, after four decades of efforts, an optimal data structure has been developed with $O(n)$ space, $O(\log n+k)$ query time and $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing time [Mat92b, Cha00, AC09, CT16]. In contrast, for a family of distance functions, the state-of-the-art data structure [AES99, KMR+20, Liu22] attains $O(n\log\log n)$ space, $O(\log n+k)$ query time and expected $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing time. An open question is the existence of an optimal data structure with $O(n)$ space and $O(\log n + k)$ query time for distance functions more general than the Euclidean metric. Such an optimal data structure also remains unknown for non-point sites in the Euclidean metric, even for disk sites or, more generally, additively weighted Euclidean distances. We develop an optimal $k$-nearest-neighbors data structure for additively weighted Euclidean distances with $O(n)$ space, $O(\log n + k)$ query time and expected $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing time. Since this data structure can be adjusted to disk sites, it serves as an initial result toward optimality for non-point sites. We also adapt our data structure to point sites under a family of convex metrics, including commonly used $L_p$ metrics and uniform orientation metrics. The data structure can be further extended to distance functions that satisfy certain axioms. Thus, we demonstrate the existence of optimal $k$-nearest-neighbors data structures for distance functions more general than point sites in the Euclidean metric. Our main technical advance is to generalize Matou\v{s}ek's shallow partition theorem for hyperplanes [Mat92b] to these settings, while achieving a logarithmic crossing number.
item.dc:creator: Chih-Hung Liu

item.title: Certified Geometry and Admissible Motion of Gerver's Sofa
item.description: arXiv:2610.13955v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The moving sofa problem asks for the largest planar set that can pass through a unit-width right-angled hallway. Gerver's 1992 construction remains the largest explicit example, but its defining switching parameters, continuum of supporting hallways, and contact topology involve transcendental equations and global inequalities. We give a reproducible exact-rational certification of the construction. A strict four-dimensional Krawczyk inclusion encloses the reduced switching system, while an independent twenty-two-dimensional Krawczyk calculation verifies Romik's full matching and contact equations in an explicit rational box. Exact interval propagation through the five analytic phases proves the support identities, global half-plane constraints, inner-wall separation, niche topology, oriented contacts, injectivity, and area bounds. From the certified support functions we identify every supporting hallway as L_t=x(t)+R_tL. For G=K_0\setminus\mathcal N(K_0) we prove directly that G is nonempty, closed, and connected and that \Phi_t(q)=R_{-t}(q-x(t)) is a continuous path in SE(2) carrying G through the hallway, with the correct initial and final arms. We further identify G with Romik's reconstruction of Gerver's classical eighteen-piece sofa. The deterministic companion verifier uses only Python's standard library and exact rational arithmetic. As a consequence, the Gerver-specific geometric hypotheses in Baek's recent variational framework are rigorously certified; we also clarify the one-sided tangent-speed convention at two contact-curve junctions.
item.dc:creator: Dawid Trela

item.title: A 0.41275 lower bound for the three-dimensional Blaschke-Lebesgue problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.13964v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that every convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ of constant width $w>0$ satisfies \[ \operatorname{Vol}(K)\ge \frac{1651}{4000}w^3=0.41275\,w^3. \] This improves the certified lower bound $0.411040473721188\ldots\,w^3$ announced by Hyra and the earlier spectral bound $4\pi w^3/33$ of Nishioka. The main new ingredient is a contact-tetrahedron estimate near equality in Jung's circumradius inequality. Four balanced contacts of a minimum circumscribed ball form a near-regular tetrahedron; constant width then forces, beyond the tetrahedron itself, spherical regions over its faces, spindle sectors along its edges, and additional face-edge sectors. These regions can be selected with pairwise disjoint interiors and quantified by the total squared-edge deficit. A sharp convexity argument relates that deficit to the circumradius, and a symmetrization argument controls the four face contributions with only quadratic loss. This gives the analytic bound $\operatorname{Vol}(K)>0.41275318$ near the Jung endpoint. For the complementary circumradius range we use Hyra's radial transport/tangent-majorant mechanism together with closed-form contact and antipodal profiles. The antipodal contribution has an elementary primitive. For the contact contribution, a second-order concavity estimate converts the angular Jacobian into an explicit rational lower density; that density is monotone in the circumradius. The whole intermediate range therefore reduces to a single endpoint calculation, giving $\operatorname{Vol}(K)>0.41275168$. For smaller circumradius the tangent-majorant inequality with its nonnegative gap discarded already gives $\operatorname{Vol}(K)>0.41308109$. The proof is entirely analytic and requires no computer-assisted certificate.
item.dc:creator: Yunjiang Jiang

item.title: Maximally symmetric $(23_4)$ configurations and the end of the existence problem for geometric $(n_4)$ configurations
item.description: arXiv:2610.14099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A geometric $(n_4)$ configuration is a set of $n$ points and $n$ lines in the real projective plane such that every point lies on exactly four of the lines and every line contains exactly four of the points. The question of which $n$ admit such a configuration was posed by Gr\"unbaum in 2000, following his 1990 paper with Rigby that gave the first geometric $4$-configuration, a $(21_4)$. Successive work of Bokowski-Schewe, of Bokowski, Gr\"unbaum and Schewe, of Bokowski-Pilaud, and of Cuntz settled every case but one. Cuntz's 2018 paper, which constructed $(22_4)$ and $(26_4)$ configurations, states that only $n=23$ remained open. We settle this last case. We prove that for every prime $n\equiv3\pmod4$, in particular for $n=23$, the group of projective symmetries of a geometric $(n_4)$ configuration has order at most four, which explains why $n=23$ resisted the symmetric constructions that settled the other values. Reducing the case of a Klein four-group of symmetries to a few thousand bilinear polynomial systems in $18$ unknowns, and solving all of them exactly with Gr\"obner bases and saturation, we show that exactly two geometric $(23_4)$ configurations reach this bound, up to projective equivalence, and that there are no others even over $\mathbb{C}$. Both are self-polar with respect to a conic. The first has integer homogeneous coordinates; the second is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17})$, but not over $\mathbb{Q}$. Consequently geometric $(n_4)$ configurations exist if and only if $n\ge18$ and $n\ne19$. A third configuration, self-polar and defined over a real cubic field, has only a single symmetry of order two. The same classification at $n=22$ and $n=26$ recovers Cuntz's configurations and finds three new combinatorial types at $n=22$ and $94$ at $n=26$, among them a $(26_4)$ configuration that is self-polar with respect to a conic without real points.
item.dc:creator: Wenhao Lu

item.title: Ellipsoids from Tangents
item.description: arXiv:2610.15580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents an algorithm for detecting and fitting multiple ellipsoids in 2D, 3D and higher-dimensional data. The representation is based on tangents to the ellipsoid together with their contact points, rather than on points alone. A tangent contributes d independent equations where a point contributes one, so each hypothesis needs fewer samples, which in turn reduces the number of iterations required to recover every ellipsoid. The problem is posed as sets of linear equations whose solutions -- the ellipsoid parameters -- are recovered robustly by clustering in parameter space. The algorithm works in all dimensions and outperforms the state of the art in 2D. The approach applies in general to the robust solution of linear equations, and so has utility beyond ellipsoid fitting.
item.dc:creator: Efrat Dahan, Michael Werman

item.title: Compositional Information Geometry of Probabilistic Programs
item.description: arXiv:2610.17886v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the compositional, intensional information geometry of probabilistic programs. For a first-order probabilistic programming language with finite random variables, we construct a contravariant lax monoidal functor that, for a program of type $X \to Y$, pulls back a (degenerate) Riemannian metric on $Y$ to $X$. It specialises to the Fisher metric in the case of standard statistical models and to ordinary pullback in the case of deterministic programs. We further justify this construction in two ways. First, we show that this functor arises as a pullback of geometry from a universal space of programs over a type $Y$ with a fixed trace space. Second, we show that it is a special case of a more general pullback construction over weighted measures. Our compositional geometry depends on the presentation of the program, and we study how it relates to the (non-compositional) geometry of the realised measures by establishing a three-level inequality relating our score-velocity metric for the program, the program's corresponding output-conditioned metric, and the standard Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric of the realised family. Finally, we show how the theory can be extended to accommodate continuous random variables using diffeological quasi-Borel spaces. We also discuss several concrete directions for future work.
item.dc:creator: Jacek Karwowski, Frank Nielsen, Sam Staton

item.title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Capacitated Stack and Queue Layouts with Colored Edges
item.description: arXiv:2610.18071v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stack and queue layouts are two extensively studied and complementary linear representations of graphs. A stack (queue) layout $\langle \prec, \sigma \rangle$ of a graph $G$ consists of a total ordering $\prec$ of its vertices and of a partitioning $\sigma$ of its edges into pages, such that no two independent edges on the same page cross (nest). We propose a generalized model with colored edges (one color per edge) and capacitated pages. Namely, the input graph is equipped with colored edges and a prescribed budget for each page-color pair $(p,c)$ - this budget determines the maximum number of edges of color $c$ that page $p$ can accept. This model is motivated by fair allocation scenarios where budgets can be used to control the share of monochromatic edges on each page. Unfortunately, it is known that deciding whether a stack (queue) layout exists is NP-hard already with two (one) pages. Thus, we focus on the fixed-order setting - where the linear order $\prec$ is part of the input - for which an ordinary 2-page stack or $\ell$-page queue layout can be computed in polynomial time. Despite the restrictive setting, we show that both capacitated problems are NP-complete already for two pages. Furthermore, we study the complexity of the problems when parameterized by the number of pages, colors, and/or the structure of the edge conflict graph with respect to the fixed linear order $\prec$. Our analysis paints a detailed complexity landscape and uncovers a surprisingly intricate interplay between the considered parameters.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Depian, Giuseppe Liotta, Fabrizio Montecchiani, Martin N\"ollenburg

item.title: A Framework for the Design of Efficient Diversification Algorithms for Packing and Covering Problems
item.description: arXiv:2501.12261v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There has been considerable recent interest in computing a diverse collection of solutions to a given optimization problem. Given a classical optimization problem $\Pi$ (e.g., minimum spanning tree, maximum independent set) with input size $n$ and an integer $k\geq 1$, the goal is to generate a collection of $k$ maximally diverse solutions to $\Pi$. This diverse-X paradigm not only allows the user to generate very different solutions, but also helps make systems more secure and robust by handling uncertainty and achieving energy efficiency. For several problems $\Pi$ solvable in polynomial time, there are efficient $\text{poly}(n,k)$-time exact or approximation algorithms available for their diverse-solution variants. In contrast, only FPT algorithms are known for NP-complete problems such as vertex covers and independent sets. In the worst case, these algorithms run in time $\exp((kn)^a)$ for some $a>0$. In this work, we address this gap and give a general framework for $\text{poly}(n,k)$-time \emph{bi-criteria} PTAS for the diverse variants of several NP-hard problems such as \textsc{Knapsack}, \textsc{Maximum Weight Independent Set} (MWIS) and \textsc{Minimum Weight Vertex Cover} (MWVC) in planar graphs. More precisely, given a maximization (or, minimization) problem $\Pi$, an integer $k \geq 1$, user-specified quality threshold $ c \in (0, 1) $, and user-controlled error parameters $\delta,\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, our bi-approximation algorithm returns a collection of $k$ solutions $S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_k$ that are $(1-\delta)c$-optimal and whose diversity is at least a $(1-\varepsilon)$-fraction of the maximum diversity achievable by any collection of $k$ $c$-optimal solutions. To complement our positive results, we prove that the diverse-solution variants of \KP and MWIS mentioned above do not admit standard single-criterion PTASs.
item.dc:creator: Waldo G\'alvez, Mayank Goswami, Arturo Merino, GiBeom Park, Meng-Tsung Tsai, Victor Verdugo

item.title: Updating zigzag representatives efficiently
item.description: arXiv:2607.16153v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Computation of zigzag persistence has progressed in recent years, with results showing that complexities of many problems closely align with those in the non-zigzag setting. The major efficiency gap now lies in the updating of zigzag representatives. In this paper, we propose efficient algorithms for updating zigzag representatives based on a recent algorithm for extracting zigzag representatives from a $R=DV$ decomposition of a constructed non-zigzag. The main difficulty for designing our update algorithms lies in the adjacency change occurring in two operations that lengthen or shorten a filtration. Despite the adjacency change, we find that the update can still be done efficiently in quadratic time.
item.dc:creator: Tamal K. Dey, Tao Hou, Dmitriy Morozov

item.title: Tight Approximation Thresholds for Geometric Stabbing
item.description: arXiv:2607.28062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study geometric covering problems: stabbing axis-parallel squares and cubes by coordinate hyperplanes, stabbing horizontal segments by horizontal and vertical lines, and transversal of separated $d$-intervals. We prove matching NP-hardness bounds for their natural covering-LP thresholds. For every $\varepsilon>0$, square stabbing is NP-hard to approximate within $2-\varepsilon$, horizontal-segment stabbing within $e/(e-1)-\varepsilon$, and, for every fixed $d\ge2$, cube stabbing and separated $d$-interval transversal within $d-\varepsilon$. The results hold with finite candidate sets and when arbitrary admissible lines, hyperplanes, or track points are allowed. We construct harmonic integrality-gap families for squares and cubes and use the Kovaleva--Spieksma gap family for horizontal segments. In each family, every object meets a candidate of every orientation. We lift these gaps through the strict-CSP framework of Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, and Vishnoi, using the Unique Games theorem to obtain NP-hardness. An ordered sampler preserves the LP marginals, coupled shifts make every local sample feasible, and a small perturbation through an absorbing label connects every local support. Cartesian cloning removes rational weights, after which disjoint blocks of candidate coordinates realize each output constraint by one square, cube, or horizontal segment. Applying the same transfer theorem to rectangle-hitting gaps of Pach and Tardos, we prove that stabbing axis-parallel boxes by supplied candidate lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is NP-hard to approximate within any fixed constant factor. Incidence-preserving algebraic maps yield the same hardness for hitting boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^6$ by points from supplied finite candidate sets.
item.dc:creator: Khaled Elbassioni, Rishikesh Gajjala, Saurabh Ray

item.title: The Geometry of the Set of Equivalent Linear Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2404.14855v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We characterize the geometry of the set of all weight vectors for which a fully-connected linear neural network computes the same linear transformation $W$. Said another way, the set of all sequences of matrices (of predetermined sizes) whose product is $W$. This set of weight vectors is an algebraic variety in the Euclidean weight space, called the fiber of $W$ under the matrix multiplication map. Sometimes this variety is a manifold, but usually not. The rank stratification of a fiber is a natural partition of the fiber into smooth manifolds of various dimensions called strata. We derive the dimensions of these strata and characterize how they are connected to each other. They satisfy the frontier condition: if a stratum intersects the closure of another stratum, then the former stratum is a subset of the closure of the latter stratum. This subset relationship can be expressed as a partial order with a single minimal element, a stratum that is included in the closure of every other stratum. Hence the strata can be arranged in a hierarchy represented by a directed acyclic graph that represents that partial order; we give an algorithm that computes that graph. A key result describes the relationship between this partial order and the ranks of certain matrices in the network. We derive the tangent and normal subspaces of the strata, and we construct elegant bases for those subspaces. Each stratum represents a different pattern of information flow through the network, expressed as a barcode, borrowed from the study of persistent homology. The topology of a stratum depends solely on its barcode. So does its geometry, up to a linear transformation in weight space. Connections among the strata are best understood through "barcode moves," which can be expressed as simple modifications of the barcodes.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Richard Shewchuk, Sagnik Bhattacharya

item.title: The Origami flip graph of the $2\times n$ Miura-ori
item.description: arXiv:2506.19700v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given an origami crease pattern $C=(V,E)$, a straight-line planar graph embedded in a region of $\mathbb{R}^2$, we assign each crease to be either a mountain crease (which bends convexly) or a valley crease (which bends concavely), creating a mountain-valley (MV) assignment $\mu:E\to\{-1,1\}$. An MV assignment $\mu$ is locally valid if the faces around each vertex in $C$ can be folded flat under $\mu$. In this paper, we investigate locally valid MV assignments of the Miura-ori, $M_{m,n}$, an $m\times n$ parallelogram tessellation used in numerous engineering applications. The origami flip graph $OFG(C)$ of $C$ is a graph whose vertices are locally valid MV assignments of $C$, and two vertices are adjacent if they differ by a face flip, an operation that swaps the MV-parity of every crease bordering a given face of $C$. We enumerate the number of vertices and edges in $OFG(M_{2,n})$ and prove several facts about the degrees of vertices in $OFG(M_{2,n})$. By finding recurrence relations, we show that the number of vertices of degree $d$ and $2n-a$ (for $0\leq a$) are both described by polynomials of particular degrees. We then prove that the diameter of $OFG(M_{2,n})$ is $\lceil \frac{n^2}{2}\rceil$ and find lower bounds on the diameter of $OFG(M_{m,n})$ using techniques from $3$-coloring reconfiguration graphs.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications, Vol. 30, No. 1 (2026), 421-444
item.dc:creator: Lumi Christensen, Thomas C. Hull, Emma O'Neil, Valentina Pappano, Natalya Ter-Saakov, Kacey Yang

item.title: A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2609.01682v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Albertson's conjecture states that every graph of chromatic number r has crossing number at least that of the complete graph K_r. We prove the conjecture for all r. The proof combines new clique-sensitive edge bounds for critical graphs, maximum-clique sampling, and a reserved immersion construction. For graphs of order close to r, we construct edge-disjoint routes while preserving a complete bipartite subgraph whose forced crossings compensate for those introduced when the immersion is smoothed into a drawing. For larger orders, we derive explicit edge bounds using independent-triple deletion and structural properties of critical graphs, then combine them with sampling inequalities that account for crossings within a maximum clique. The remaining numerical inequalities are certified using exact rational arithmetic, with a reproducible certificate and standalone Python verifier.
item.dc:creator: Ankan Sadhu

item.title: Overlap-Helly theorems
item.description: arXiv:2609.10023v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper we introduce a generalization of Helly's theorem closely connected to B\'ar\'any-Gromov overlap theorems (also called selection lemmas). Our main result implies both the topological colorful Helly of Kalai and Meschulam and Karasev's topological centerpoint theorem. We further investigate the topological fractional Helly theorem from this overlap perspective, and show an overlap theorem for dense complexes (a continuous second selection lemma for tame maps).
item.dc:creator: Andreas F. Holmsen, Alfredo Hubard

item.title: Simple symmetric Venn diagrams with 17, 19 and 23 curves
item.description: arXiv:2609.26546v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We exhibit simple, rotationally symmetric Venn diagrams with 17 curves, with 19 curves and with 23 curves: $n$ Jordan curves carried to one another by rotation through $2\pi/n$, with every one of the $2^n$ regions present and connected and, since the diagrams are simple, every crossing on exactly two curves. Symmetric Venn diagrams exist for every prime number of curves (Griggs, Killian and Savage, 2004), but those diagrams have many curves through a point; simple ones were known only up to 13 curves (Mamakani and Ruskey, 2014). Four 17-curve, twelve 19-curve and six 23-curve diagrams were found by a Metropolis walk on rotation-invariant quadrangulations of the sphere in which regions may temporarily be duplicated, started from the Griggs-Killian-Savage diagram with its multiple crossings resolved. At 23 curves the walk was held for two weeks by duplicated regions near the poles; the two lineages that finished were the first whose $E=92$ states had none. Every diagram is given by a machine-checkable certificate; one certificate each of the 17-, 19- and 23-curve sizes has been verified by a formal proof in Lean 4. All of the diagrams are non-monotone, which is why the crossing-sequence searches that found the 11- and 13-curve diagrams could not have found them.
